full_judgment:
2. This arises from Title Suit No.201 of 1963 of the 3rd Court of Munsif, Comilla. The suit land, which appertained to C.S. Plots Nos. 675 and 678 of Mouza Chatura, belonged to defendant No 2. Delaney Estate which possessed it in khas. The plaintiff purchased it by a registered kabala dated 1, August 1959, went into possession and made some constructions including pucca boundary pillars. But on 12 August 1963 defendantNo.1; the respondent before us, forcibly dispossessed him from this land setting up a claim of title on the basis of purchase under a registered kabala dated 11 July 1963 from one Rabi Dasi, daughter of one Biman Dasi. Defendant No.1 claimed that Biman Dasi took lease of 10 decimals of land including the suit land from the Delaney Estate by executing kabuliyat in the year 1935 and that after possessing it for many years she gifted it to her daughter, Rabi Dasi, by a deed of gift dated 6-9-62. The lease of Biman Dasi, it was alleged by defendant No.1, was for 10 decimals of land, but in the lease-deed the area was wrongly stated to be 'one' decimal instead of 10 decimals; nevertheless, the lease was acted upon in respect of the whole area and the land was all along in possession of the lessee. The plaintiff denied tae alleged mis-description in the lease-deed and led evidence to show that on a previous occasion the vendor of defendant No.1 had dispossessed the Delaney Estate from the suit land whereupon possession was recovered and title of the landlord was declared by a decree passed in Title Suit No.128 of 1965. Defendant No 1 contended that the suit land covered by the decree in the previous title suit was different from the subject-matter of the instant suit. But a Pleader Commissioner who held a local investigation, submitted a report finding that the lands under both the suits are same and identical. 

 4. A second appeal was preferred against that Judgment-S.A. No. 220 of 1963 in whicha contention was raised for the first time that the transfer by Delaney Estate to the plaintiff under the kabala dated 1.8.59 was hit by section 9(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Section 9(1) put an embargo on transfer, without previous permission of the Government, by private sale or gift, of any interest in an estate, or tenure or transfer of any land in khas possession of a rent-receiver whose rent-receiving interests were acquired by a notification under section 3(1) of the S ate Acquisition and Tenancy Act. But since this question was not raised during the trial, or even before the lower appellate court, the plaintiff got no opportunity to adduce evidence whether the transfer was made with the required permission. The High Court Division therefore sent the case on remand for determination of this question only. But the plaintiff feeling aggrieved moved this Court and obtained leave to appeal from that order for remand contending that in view of subsequent amendments of section 9(1) the requirement of previous permission for transfer of any land not exceeding 10 bighas was done away with and consequently the transfer was perfectly valid. 

 5. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan learned Advocate for the plaintiff appellant, has produced before us a number of subsequent Amendments of section 9(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act two of which are relevant in this case. These are East Pakistan Ordinance No. 14 of 1957, dated 15 August 1957 and East Pakistan Ordinance No. 27 of 1961 dated 7 August 1961. Original section 9 ran thus: 

 "(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on and from the date of publication of a notification under sub-section (I) of section 3, no rent receiver specified in such notification shall, except with the previous permission of a prescribed authority transfer his rights and interests in any estate, taluk or "tenure, to which such notification relates, by private sale, gift, will, mortgage, lease or any contract or agreement, or transfer any land in his khas possession by any such means. 

 6. M.H Khondkar, learned Advocate for the respondent, bas however contended that the suit land is not an 'agricultural land' but it is a "non-agricultural land," and as such the amendment does not save" the appellant's transfer from the mischief of law. But this question whether the suit land is a non-agricultural land was not raised either before the trial Court or before the lower Appellate Court and it is for the first time before the High Court Division in second appeal that this question was raised. Contention of Mr. M.H. Khondkar, is that a question of law may be raised at any stage of a proceeding including a proceeding before the Appellate Division. There is hardly any dispute that a question of law may be raised at any stage of a proceeding. But if the determination or a question of law is dependent upon prior determination of a question of fact then this principle of law will not be applicable., Whether the land is 'agricultural land' or 'non-agricultural land' is a question of fact and this question not having been raised in the written statement or at any stage prior to the filing of the second appeal cannot be" entertained now. Even if the suit land is taken as a non-agricultural land for the sake of argument, still the transfer in question will not be invalid in view of the further amendment of section 9(1) brought about by East Pakistan Ordinance No.27 of 1961. This amendment has done away with the provision for prior permission for transfer of any land, whether agricultural or non-agricultural, not exceeding ten standard bighas with retrospective effect from the date of corning into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act itself. By this Ordinance, original section 9 has been replaced and a new section has been substituted which is quoted below: 

 (1) of section 3, no rent-receiver, specified in such notification shall except as provided in sub-section (la), transfer his rights and interests in any estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy, to which such notification relates, by private sale, gift, will, mortgage, lease or any contract or agreement, or transfer any land in his khas possession by any such means without the previous permission of a prescribed authority. 

 "The position, therefore, is that....... section 9 of the original Act must be read to have always been as stated in section 3 of the Ordinance. Therefore, this is irresistible conclusion that section 3 of the Ordinance which replaced section 9 of the Act, has retrospective effect ab initio."
